A close look at the unfolded light curve shows that alternating eclipses (odd and even) are of different depths, so this one is a clear stellar eclipsing binary at 4.2 days. Light curve also shows quarter to quarter depth variations, and inter-quarter trend in eclipses depth. Possible nearby companion = Yes (1.49" companion (UKIRT))

I tried to observe this at Lick, and found four stars within 4 arcseconds. Each star is individually much fainter than the Kep_mag = 13.8. The individual magnitudes are probably closer to 15-16th magnitude. I did not take any spectra, but did take this screen capture from the guide camera. The bright star in the DSS is visible. Note that East is left, but North is down. Of the four stars, the top and bottom star are separated by about 8 arcseconds. 667Ic-hi20100802.jpg Possible nearby companion = Yes (2.92" companion (UKIRT)) Possible false positive = No (disposition updated) Possible nearby companion = Yes (2.94" companion (UBV, UKIRT))

An image taken with the Lick Observatory 1-m Nickel Telescope is available in .pdf and .fits format. Each pdf has a 1.2'x1.2' view centered on the star, and a close-up view of the star in an 11"x11" field. The seeing is ~ 1.5". No companions visible from 2" to 5" away from the star down to 19th magnitude. 579Ic-hi20100711.pdf McDonald 60K recon. phase = 0.74. No spectrum -- lost it to clouds! McD 31 Aug/1 Sep 2010 Teff=5000 K, log(g)=5.0, Vrot=0 km/s, Vrad=-39.270 km/s, phase=0.74 579C-sq20120727a.ps As Bill says, the spectrum was aborted due to clouds, but the short exposure before that happened isn't completely useless. The spectrum is weak and noisy and the correlation coefficient is only 0.326, but the velocity might still be good enough to reveal a stellar companion. I wouldn't put much stock in the results though, and we might decide later that we need to re-observe this phase. For now, let's get an observation at the opposite quadrature. I examined carefully your list: EB_KOI_match_active.txt to identify any KOIs for which we were obtaining precise RVs that were also thought to be EBs. The stars with precise RVs noted as being both a KOI and EB: 261 1661 (CBP, = Kepler 16) For KOI-261, our RVs show no evidence of a binary. The RVs span 400 days and have an RMS 3.0 m/s relative to the possible linear downward trend (~7 m/s during the past year) during the past year. In contrast, an eclipsing binary with P=16.24 d would have orbital speeds of ~100 km/s, 4 orders of magnitude faster than we measure. Thus, most of the light (99.9%) comes from a star that is *not* an eclipsing binary. High Precision Radial Velocites from Keck/HIRES, uploaded Dec 2011. Note from observation request: single transit; 0.23 R_j We saw, on the HIRES guider, a star about 3 mag fainter located 1.3 " away. Steve Howell reports K42 has a fainter companion barely in our box at about 1.2" away, no doubt the same companion seen on the HIRES guider (noted 2009-06-13). Spectroscopy is possible only in good seeing. Teff=6250, log(g)=4.0, Vrot=16, Vrad=-41.18 One McDonald 2.7-m coude spectrum from 2454989.9274 42Sp-DL090607.ps 42Lp-so090606.pdf Teff=6500, log(g)=4.0, Vrot=16, Vrad=-40.16 One TRES spectrum. What do the HIRES velocities show? If the HIRES template exposure can be uploaded, Lars can run his classification analysis. 42Sp-dl090614.ps Per FOP telecon: Waiting to see HIRES results. Possible trouble from nearby companion. No centroid data yet. Is bright so would be nice for a planet. Leave at FOP P2. HIRES RV using telluric lines (0.13 km/s): On BJD = 2454988.9797, RV = -39.966 km/s This RV is 0.2 km/s higher than from TRES, but 1.2 km/s higher than from McD. The companion 1.2" away makes this KOI too seeing-dependent for reliable follow-up, in my view. P2 probably should become P3. Per FOP telecon of 090722: Star only 2.2 mag fainter within 1.2" makes this a difficult star to get good HIRES measurements on. Keep at FOP priority 3 and wait for more photometry and centroid work. Consider Spitzer observations. This is on hold for now, but let's keep it on the active list, because it is so bright. We may decide it is worth a special effort some time in the future. The data are not statistically significant, but both "g" and "r" reconstructed images show a suspicious looking thing at the same separation and PA. It is certainly on the re-observe list. KOI-42 had Q1 SC data enabling an early asteroseismic analysis. Jørgen and Hans have exercised the KASOC pipeline on KOI-42 resulting in clear detection of 18 individual frequencies and clear identification of l = 0, 1, and 2 modes. Following computation of stellar evolution models over a suitable mass range, and assuming [Fe/H] = -0.3,0,0.3 it is possible to select models within 2 sigma of T_eff (6000 to 6800 K based on preliminary spectroscopic reports by Latham below) and constrain the mean stellar density, which is: 0.689 +/- 0.017 g/cm^3. Only relatively weak constraints on mass and radius separately follow: M = 1.2 +/- 0.2, R = 1.34 +/- 0.06 solar. Current modeling does not yet provide good solutions for the individual frequencies, the quoted stellar density is based on the observed large separation. Key information needed are improved quantities from spectroscopy: T_eff, [Fe/H] and Vsini is also important since in the 16 km/s range of the initial solution confusion of modes given the substantial influence of rotation is possible. The procedure is roughly this: 1) An SME or SPC solution for Teff and [Fe/H] was provided by Debra Fischer or Lars Buchhave using available spectroscopy. 2) The SC time series were analyzed by several members of KASOC returning the global oscillation parameters giving the mean separation between successive modes and the frequency of peak power. 3) The global oscillations parameters are used in a stellar evolution grid-based solution yielding most fundamentally the mean stellar density, but also radius, mass and in this case log(g). 4) The resulting asteroseismic based log(g) is then adopted by Debra (SME) or Lars (SPC) as a prior for a new spectroscopic solution for Teff and [Fe/H] in particular. 5) Using the new, iterated Teff and [Fe/H] the global oscillations parameters are again used in deriving mean stellar density, radius and mass in the context of stellar evolution constraints. These results follow as the median from several independent pipelines created by multiple KASOC members. Author: Van Eylen, Vincent, et. al. Title: "What asteroseismology can do for exoplanets: Kepler-410A b is a Small Neptune around a bright star, in an eccentric orbit consistent with low obliquity" link: http://adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013arXiv1312.4938V Abstract: We confirm the Kepler planet candidate Kepler-410b (KOI-42b) as a Neptune sized exoplanet on a 17.8 day, eccentric orbit around the bright (Kp = 9.4) star Kepler-410A. This is the third brightest confirmed planet host star in the Kepler field and one of the brightest hosts of all currently known transiting exoplanets. Kepler-410 consists of a blend between the fast rotating planet host star (Kepler-410A) and a fainter star (Kepler-410B), which has complicated the confirmation of the planetary candidate. Employing asteroseismology, using constraints from the transit light curve, adaptive optics and speckle images, and Spitzer transit observations, we demonstrate that the candidate can only be an exoplanet orbiting Kepler-410A. Via asteroseismology we determine the following stellar and planetary parameters with high precision; M$_\\star = 1.214 \\pm 0.033$ M$_\\odot$, R$_\\star = 1.352 \\pm 0.010$ R$_\\odot$, Age = $2.76 \\pm 0.54$ Gyr, planetary radius ($2.838 \\pm 0.054$ R$_\\oplus$), and orbital eccentricity ($0.17^{+0.07}_{-0.06}$). In addition, rotational splitting of the pulsation modes allows for a measurement of Kepler-410A's inclination and rotation rate. Our measurement of an inclination of $82.5^{+7.5}_{-2.5}$ [$^\\circ$] indicates a low obliquity in this system. Transit timing variations indicate the presence of at least one additional (non-transiting) planet in the system. Let's see what the McDonald spectrum shows. McD 29/30 Sep 2010 Teff=6000 K, log(g)=4.5, Vrot=4 km/s, Vrad=-11.484 km/s 414C-sq20130313a.ps There is a large velocity variation (~20 km/s). I've double-checked the Lick observation to make sure I properly shifted the velocity. We'll have to take a closer look at this one. One comment right off the bat: the velocity variation is in phase with the ephemeris of the 5.9-day orbit but not the 20-day orbit. I would say this is bad news for the prospect of either event corresponding to a planetary companion. Here's why: the 5.9-day event is shallow (2.8 Rearth) while the 20-day event is deep (1.6 Rjup). If the shallow event is associated with a stellar companion to the primary star, then the deep event is unlikely to be a planet transiting a fainter background star. These are just initial musings, and two RVs are obviously far from conclusive evidence. Somebody should look at this system in detail. Since I'm assigned to review the multiples, I'll bring it up at the first FOP KOI review. Possible nearby companion = Yes (2.96" companion (UKIRT)) I happened to notice this star shows no starspot activity, despite being mid-G. Given the opportunity, I decided to check for phase variations (as in http://arxiv.org/abs/1106.2713, etc). I phased the data to the ephemeris and split it into 100 bins, averaged the data per bin, and plotted them. There is not much variation, and all three phase modulations have amplitudes compatible with zero. There is a slight tail of non-zero solutions for the doppler boosting amplitude, which is caused by a few moderate outliers towards phase 0.8; the rest of the data do not support this, and the distribution is not distinct from zero, so this is not significant. Due to the relatively long orbital period, doppler boosting is more constraining of the companion mass than ellipsoidal variations. If my calculations are correct, The boosting amplitude is Using the value of a/R given in the most recent DV report (16.46 ± 0.42), one derives an implied stellar density of 1.31 ± 0.10 g/cm^3 (assuming zero eccentricity and negligible companion mass), which is reasonably compatible with the KIC Teff. So, this seems like a good planet candidate. The star is very faint, so I imagine follow-up would be difficult, but presumably validation would be possible.
